intro.html: How do we know what we know? Scientists, judges, detectives and careful readers all use the same small set of words for testing ideas: you start with a hypothesis or a premise, gather empirical evidence, see whether others corroborate it, and decide whether the result is conclusive. These words turn up constantly in the science and history passages of reading tests.

Starting points: hypothesis (an idea to test), premise (a statement you reason from). Kinds of evidence: empirical (observed, measured), anecdotal (stories). Backing it up: corroborate, substantiate, validate. Reaching an answer: deduce (reason it out), extrapolate (extend beyond the data), conclusive (settles it).

words.def: based on observation or experiment, not on theory alone
words.ex: Sami gathered {empirical} evidence by timing how long each paper airplane stayed in the air.
words.ctx: The claim sounded convincing, but it had no {empirical} support: no one had ever tested it, measured anything or watched it happen.

mn.text: Don’t just guess how many seeds will sprout: peer at them, count them, write it down. Knowledge you get by peering and testing is {empirical}.

scene.alt: A girl in a lab coat peers through a magnifying glass at sprouting plants.

words.def: based on personal stories rather than careful study
words.ex: The only proof that the shortcut was faster was {anecdotal}: Dev said it felt quicker.
words.ctx: Several fishermen swore that the biggest trout bit only on rainy days, but the evidence was merely {anecdotal}; no one had ever kept a careful record of the catches.
words.etym: From Greek anekdota, “things not published”: an (not) + ekdotos (given out); an anecdote began as a private, untold story.

mn.text: Annie swears her lucky socks win every game. Her only proof is Annie’s tale about last Saturday, not a count of wins and losses. Her evidence is {anecdotal}.

scene.alt: A girl holds up her lucky sock and tells a story, while a scientist wonders where the data is.

words.def: to confirm or support with more evidence
words.ex: Two neighbors {corroborated} the boy’s story about the runaway goat.
words.ctx: At first only one hiker reported seeing the rare owl, but photos from three other hikers soon {corroborated} her account.
words.etym: From Latin corroborare, “to strengthen”: cor (thoroughly) + roborare (to make strong), from robur, oak, strength.

mn.cue: co-ROB: a CO-REPORT backs it up
mn.text: “The goat ate my sock!” says Kai. “I saw it too!” says Maya, pointing at the sock in the goat’s mouth. Her second report helps {corroborate} his story.

scene.alt: A boy says a goat ate his sock, and a girl points at the goat and says she saw it too.

words.def: to support a claim with proof
words.ex: Can you {substantiate} your claim that the cafeteria pizza is getting smaller?
words.ctx: The scientist’s bold theory was exciting, but she could not yet {substantiate} it; until her experiments produced solid data, other researchers stayed doubtful.
words.etym: From substance, Latin substantia, “that which stands under”: the solid stuff beneath a thing.

mn.cue: SUB-STAN-tiate: solid ground to STAND on
mn.text: A claim needs something solid to stand on. Dev backs up “The pizza shrank!” with a ruler and last month’s photo. Now he can {substantiate} it.

scene.alt: A boy measures a pizza with a ruler to prove it has shrunk, next to a photo from last month.

words.def: to check or prove that something is sound or correct
words.ex: The lab ran the test three more times to {validate} the surprising result.
words.ctx: The new trail map looked accurate, but the rangers wanted to {validate} it before printing it, so they walked every path with a compass and the old survey.
words.etym: From Latin validus, “strong,” from valere, “to be strong, to be worth.”

mn.text: The conductor checks Nell’s ticket against the schedule and stamps it VALID. To check that something is sound and correct is to {validate} it.

scene.alt: A train conductor holds up a passenger’s ticket marked valid with a check mark.

words.ex: The muddy paw prints on the sofa were {conclusive}: the dog had been inside.
words.ctx: Earlier studies had only hinted at the answer, but this one was {conclusive}: it tested thousands of samples and left no room for doubt.
words.etym: From Latin concludere, “to close up”: con (thoroughly) + claudere (to shut).

mn.cue: con-CLUE-sive: the CLUE that closes the case
mn.text: Muddy paw prints lead from the door straight to the dog asleep on the sofa: the last clue that closes the case. The evidence is {conclusive}.

scene.alt: A boy detective with a magnifying glass follows muddy prints to a sleeping dog on the sofa.

words.def: a statement assumed true and used as a starting point for reasoning
words.ex: The whole plan rested on one {premise}: that the store would still be open at nine.
words.ctx: Her conclusion followed logically, but it was built on a false {premise}; she had assumed the bridge was open, and it had been closed for repairs all week.
words.etym: From Latin praemissa, “sent before”: prae (before) + mittere (to send); a premise is put first, before the conclusion.
words.note: In the plural, premises can also mean a building and its grounds: “No dogs on the premises.”

mn.cue: PRE-MISE: the block that goes FIRST
mn.text: An argument is a tower of blocks, and the {premise} is the block at the bottom: set down first, before anything is built on it. If it is wobbly, the whole tower falls.

scene.alt: A professor points to a stack of boxes; the bottom one is labeled premise and the top one conclusion.

words.def: to reach a conclusion by reasoning from facts
words.ex: From the crumbs on his shirt, Mom {deduced} who had eaten the last cookie.
words.ctx: No one told the detective where the thief had gone, but she {deduced} it from the clues: wet footprints, an open window and a missing umbrella.
words.etym: From Latin deducere, “to lead down”: de (down, from) + ducere (to lead); reasoning leads you from the facts to the answer.

mn.text: The bread is gone, and one duck has crumbs all over its beak. Zoe didn’t see it happen, but she can {deduce} who ate it.

scene.alt: A girl with an empty bread bag points at the duck with crumbs on its beak.

words.def: to use known facts or trends to predict what lies beyond them
words.ex: From three weeks of growth, Lin {extrapolated} that her sunflower would top the fence by August.
words.ctx: The town had grown by about a hundred people a year for a decade, so planners {extrapolated} from that trend to estimate how many classrooms they would need in ten years.
words.etym: Formed from extra (beyond) and the ending of interpolate, “to fill in between known points.”

mn.cue: EXTRA-polate: draw the line EXTRA far
mn.text: Lin’s sunflower grew a foot each week, so she draws the line extra far, past what she has measured: “By August it will beat the fence!” To predict that way is to {extrapolate}.

cast.think: By August: TALLER than the fence!

scene.alt: A woman with a ruler imagines her sunflower growing taller than the fence by August.

words.def: a proposed explanation that can be tested
words.ex: Kai’s {hypothesis} was that plants given music would grow taller.
words.ctx: Every test so far had matched her {hypothesis}, but the scientist kept experimenting, knowing that one careful result could still prove her idea wrong.
words.etym: From Greek hypothesis, “a foundation, a supposition”: hypo (under) + thesis (a placing).

mn.cue: HYPO = UNDER: an idea put UNDER a test
mn.text: Kai guesses that music helps plants grow, so he plays songs to one plant and not to the other. A guess that you put under a test is a {hypothesis}.

scene.alt: A boy wonders whether music helps plants grow, testing a plant beside a radio against one without.

head: step
word
example
rows: All the plants got the same water.
A second class gets the same result.
So the music made the difference.
A year of music would double their height?
Many careful tests agree; no doubt remains.
after.cap: The words of a fair test, in order.

after.html: Anecdotal evidence is real (the stories happened), but there are too few stories, or they are too hand-picked, to prove a pattern. Extrapolate reaches beyond the data you have; interpolate fills in between data points you already have.

items.q: Three friends say the new shoes made them run faster, but no one timed them. Their evidence is…
items.why: Personal stories without careful measurement are anecdotal evidence. Timing the runs would make it empirical.

items.q: A scientist has measurements for 2010 through 2020 and uses them to predict 2030. She is…
items.why: Predicting beyond the range of the data is extrapolating. Estimating a value between 2010 and 2020 would be interpolating.

items.q: True or false: in an argument, the premise comes at the end.
items.why: False. A premise (from Latin “sent before”) is the starting statement; the conclusion comes at the end.

items.q: The security camera footage ______ the witness’s account. Which word fits?
items.why: Footage that confirms what a witness said corroborates it: it adds supporting evidence.
